extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical/projective geometry (readers of 19th-century mathematical exposition)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of projective/modern-geometry concepts (anharmonic ratio, section of involution, connections with sines/angles/dihedral angles, and an elimination method example), aimed at explaining definitions, theorems, and constructive/coordinate proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three coincident forms of the anharmonic ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: If any four points a, b, c, d are taken on a straight line, and any two are considered as primarily conjugate to each other and the other two secondarily conjugate, then there are three coincident forms of the anharmonic ratio; any one of these forms implies the other two. All twelve pairwise combinations collapse effectively into these three types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates the twelve combinatory pairs and groups them into three equivalent classes (marked (1),(2),(3)), and notes these correspond to relative arrangements of the radiants. This is the foundational combinatorial statement about cross-ratio forms used throughout the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus fundamental property for transversals (cross-ratio relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two transversals are cut by four radiants in a, b, c, d and a', b', c', d' respectively, there is a fundamental algebraic relation among the corresponding segment ratios (the Pappus theorem form) giving equalities of anharmonic ratios for the two transversals; any one of these equalities implies the other two, and the same is true for their reciprocals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement is given as the key geometric property from which many consequences follow; the reader is referred to Hutton (vol. ii) for demonstrations. The property underlies later formulae relating segments and angles/sines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of segment ratios to sines of angles (line case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For four radiants A,B,C,D meeting at a point and a transversal cutting them in a,b,c,d, the segment ratios satisfy relations expressible in sines of the angles formed at the common origin: e.g. ac:be = sin(AC):sin(BC), ad:bd = sin(AD):sin(BD), and analogous equalities for the other pairings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved (Hutton, ii, p.239–241) by similarity/triangle arguments; these relations are immediately useful for passing between segment cross-ratio and angular data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to planes and dihedral angles
rubrics_metrics.description: If four planes A,B,C,D meet in a line and are cut by a transversal in points a,b,c,d, then the same sine-relations hold between segments of the transversal and the dihedral angles of the planes (replace plane-angles by dihedral angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction obtained by constructing an auxiliary perpendicular plane through the intersection line and transferring the line-case argument to dihedral angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to great circles on the sphere (spherical case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For four great circles meeting at a point on a sphere and a transversal great circle cutting them in a,b,c,d, the relations among sines of arcs hold: sin(ac):sin(be) = sin(AC):sin(BC), and analogous formulae for the other pairings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by reducing the spherical case to the planar case via central planes through the great circles; substitution ac = 2 sin(arc/2) is used in conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skew-lines (three non-coplanar lines) property / hyperboloid case
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any three lines L, L', L'' no two coplanar (which admit infinitely many common transversals, generating a one-sheeted hyperboloid), the segments cut upon these three lines by any four transversal lines that rest on them have the same anharmonic ratios: i.e., the anharmonic ratio is invariant for corresponding segments on the three skew lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is established following Chasles' method (see Hutton vol. ii p.243) and ties projective cross-ratio invariance to the geometry of ruled surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectibility / invariance under radial projection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line abcd is radially projected onto any plane or onto any other line, the anharmonic ratio of the projection equals that of the original line; radial projection preserves the anharmonic ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as the foundation of the projectibility of lines and foundational for methods that transfer problems between configurations by projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's algebraic relation for four collinear points
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the three relative arrangements (figures (1),(2),(3)), the four points satisfy one of three algebraic relations among segment products: (1) ab·cd − ac·bd + be·ad = 0; (2) ab·cd + ac·bd + be·ad = 0; (3) ab·cd − ac·bd − be·ad = 0. In a canonical ordering this reduces to ab·cd + be·ad = ac·bd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identities are useful algebraic forms equivalent to cross-ratio equalities and are credited to Euler (New Petersburgh Commentaries, 1747–8); proofs are given by direct manipulation of segment sums in the three figure types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of anharmonic ratio via two cutting lines (two-transversal formulae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the Euler theorem and the relations of (II), the anharmonic ratio for four points on a transversal may be expressed in terms of the segments of two (or several) other lines cutting the same radiants; several symmetric equations exist and any one implies the other two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These multi-line expressions are derived by composing Euler's relations and the fundamental anharmonic system of radiants; they facilitate computation of cross-ratios from alternate intercepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate theorem: moving lines about poles describe a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two fixed lines OE and O'E' with chosen poles P,P', and two revolving lines through P,P' cutting OE and O'E' in a, a' respectively satisfying a linear fractional condition (expressed as (Oa/Ka) + (O'a'/K'a') = constant), the intersection point Q of the two revolving lines describes a conic section passing through the poles P,P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A coordinate derivation is provided: by taking OE and O'E' as axes, substituting parametric line equations, and eliminating parameters one obtains a general second-degree equation (a conic). The relation will be connected later to the anharmonic ratio method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of section of involution (and centre / foci of involution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of pairs (a,a'), (b,b'), (c,c'), ... on a line are in involution (the line is a section of involution) relative to a given point o if oa·oa' = ob·ob' = oc·oc' = ... ; the point o is the centre of involution. Two points w,w' at equal distances from o with wo·ow' = ao·oa' are called focal points of the involution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition follows Chasles' conception and is chosen for constructive clarity; it connects Desargues' and Pappus' earlier treatments to a simple multiplicative condition about distances from a centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic relations among midpoints and segments for involution
rubrics_metrics.description: If three pairs a/a', b/b', c/c' are in involution and m is any point with ma, ma', mb, mb', mc, mc' distances as given, then identities such as ma·ma'·By − mb·mb'·ya + mc·mc'·aB = 0 hold (where By, ya, aB denote mid-segment differences). Similar equivalent algebraic identities are derived and shown to hold for any choice of m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs proceed by expanding ma·ma' etc. as quadratic polynomials in mo (distance from m to centre) and using Euler-type relations together with the defining equalities oa·oa' = ob·ob' etc.; the identities are useful in applications and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven canonical relations for six points in involution
rubrics_metrics.description: If three points a,b,c and their conjugates a',b',c' form an involution of six points, a canonical system of seven multiplicative relations among the segments holds (the text lists these seven symmetric equations). The first three were discovered by Desargues; the remaining four are those given by Pappus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of the seven equations implies that the line is divided in involution and in turn implies the other six; composition/multiplication of pairwise defining equalities produces the full system. The text outlines how to derive the later ones by combining the first three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chasles' memorization rule for composing Desargues/Apollonius formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule: When taking three points a,b,c from three couples, each makes two segments with the conjugates of the two others, giving six segments; the product of three of these segments which have no common extremity equals the product of the three others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a convenient mnemonic for writing down the involution-formulae (Desargues/Apollonius), facilitating symmetric ordering and error checking when forming the relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of involution by equality of anharmonic ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain specified anharmonic ratios formed from the six points (various listed systems such as a' b e a equal to ab' c' a, etc.) are equal to their conjugates, then the six points are in involution; conversely, if the points are in involution these anharmonic ratios are equal. From one such equality two others follow, producing a total of eighteen related equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The converse and equivalence are established by manipulation of the Desargues/Apollonius equations; the author recommends tabulating the 18 equations for future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination procedure for differential equations (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two differential equations P(x, y, φ, φ', φ'', ...) = 0 and Q(...) = 0 of the same order in the auxiliary function φ, substitute expressions for derivatives to express φ-derivatives in terms of x,y and derivatives of y; combine P and Q to eliminate the highest derivative of φ obtaining an intermediate equation; differentiate repeatedly and use combinations with P or Q to lower the maximal derivative order of φ stepwise until φ is eliminated, yielding an equation involving only x,y and derivatives of y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives a general algorithmic outline and illustrates it with the classical mechanical example (equations of motion), showing intermediate simplifications, identification of curvature/radius p, and derivation of known dynamical relations; it remarks on order-reduction by differentiation and elimination at each stage.
